courses.title: Data Structures & Algorithms
courses.blurb: From what an algorithm is to advanced graphs, tries, greedy, intervals and advanced dynamic programming: every idea explained from first principles, with diagrams, code in several languages, complexity tables and practice problems.
courses.intro:
## How this course works

Each lesson follows the same shape, so you always know where you are:

1. **Intuition** in plain words, with a picture, before any code.
2. **How it works**, step by step on a small example.
3. **Code** you can read in JavaScript, Python, Java or C++ (pick a tab).
4. **Complexity** as a table: what each operation costs in time and space, and why.
5. **Practice**: hand-picked problems from the PrepOS problem bank, then a three-question check.

## How to study

- Go in order the first time. Later chapters assume the earlier ones.
- Read the intuition, then **close the page and try to explain it aloud** before reading the code.
- Type the code yourself. Reading code feels like understanding; typing it is understanding.
- Solve the linked problems before moving on. A lesson is only really done when you can solve a problem that uses it.
- Mark a lesson done only after the check. Your progress here is separate from your daily plan and never affects your streak.

## The big picture

Almost every interview problem is one of a few **patterns** on top of a few **data structures**. The chapters go: measuring cost (Big-O), then arrays and hashing, then the pointer and window patterns, binary search, and onward to trees, graphs and dynamic programming.

courses.title: System Design (HLD + LLD)
courses.blurb: Every system design topic taught twice, high-level and low-level: building blocks, data and messaging, reliability, distributed systems (consensus, transactions, CAP) and full interview case studies.
courses.audience: Backend engineers preparing for design interviews
courses.intro:
## HLD and LLD, side by side

Interviewers ask system design in two flavours, and good engineers need both:

- **HLD (high-level design)**: boxes and arrows. Which services, databases, caches and queues? How does it scale to millions of users? What breaks, and what do you trade away?
- **LLD (low-level design)**: classes and code. What are the entities, interfaces and design patterns? How do you make it thread-safe and testable?

Every lesson here has an **HLD** tab and an **LLD** tab for the same topic, so you learn how the big picture turns into real code.

## How to use it

1. Read the HLD tab and try to sketch the diagram yourself first.
2. Read the LLD tab and implement the core classes from memory.
3. Take the check, then open the matching case study under System Design for a full 45-minute mock.

Numbers to keep in mind throughout: a server handles roughly thousands of requests per second, memory is about 100 ns, SSD about 100 us, a cross-region network hop about 100 ms.

courses.title: Frontend Engineering at Scale
courses.blurb: How the browser really works, rendering strategies, React in depth (rendering model, Server Components, concurrency), Core Web Vitals and performance, testing, accessibility and security, and frontend architecture at scale.
courses.audience: Frontend and full-stack engineers going from mid-level to senior
courses.intro:
## What this course is for

Most frontend interviews past the junior level stop asking what a hook does and start asking **why**: why the page is slow, why this rendering strategy, why this state library, how fifty engineers ship one frontend without breaking each other. This course teaches the reasoning behind those answers.

## How each lesson works

1. **Concepts** in plain words, with a diagram, before any code.
2. **How it works** underneath: what the browser, the framework or the build tool actually does.
3. **In code**: TypeScript and React you can read and type yourself.
4. **Interview**: the questions senior candidates get, with model answers.
5. A three-question **check** before you mark the lesson done.

## How to study

- Chapter 1 (the browser and rendering) is the foundation; take it in order.
- Chapter 2 (architecture at scale) is what separates senior answers. Read it alongside the *Frontend at scale* and *Frontend system design* tracks under Web & AI, and build one of their projects.
- After each lesson, close the page and explain the main diagram out loud in two minutes. If you cannot, read it again.

Your progress here is separate from the daily plan and never affects your streak.

courses.title: GenAI End to End
courses.blurb: From how an LLM turns tokens into the next token, through training and serving, to RAG in depth, agents and tool calling with MCP, and shipping safely with evals, observability, guardrails and cost control.
courses.intro:
## What this course is for

AI-engineer interviews now mix three kinds of question: **how the model works** (attention, training, sampling, the KV cache), **how to build with it** (RAG, tools, agents) and **how to ship it** (evals, safety, cost and latency). This course covers all three in the order you need them.

## How each lesson works

1. **Concepts** first, with diagrams and small worked examples.
2. **Under the hood**: the maths and the systems, explained in plain words with shapes and numbers.
3. **In code**: Python and TypeScript you can run and change.
4. **Interview**: questions and model answers.
5. A three-question **check** before you mark it done.

## How to study

- Chapter 1 explains the model. You do not need to train one, but you must be able to explain the forward pass, why the KV cache exists and what temperature does.
- Chapter 2 is about building. Pair it with the *RAG and AI search* and *GenAI engineering* tracks under Web & AI, and build the RAG assistant or the research agent project: an AI project with real evals is the strongest resume line right now.
- The field moves fast. The ideas here are stable; check provider docs for the exact API details before you use them.

Your progress here is separate from the daily plan and never affects your streak.

courses.title: Backend Engineering
courses.blurb: HTTP and API design, authentication and security, the Node.js runtime, databases and caching, queues, testing and production operations: everything a backend engineer is asked in interviews and needs on the job.
courses.audience: Developers moving from tutorials to production-grade backend work
courses.intro:
## What this course is for

Backend interviews and real backend work reward the same thing: knowing **what happens underneath** a request. Why is this endpoint slow? Why did the retry charge the customer twice? Why does the server freeze under load? This course teaches the mechanics and the judgement behind those answers.

## How each lesson works

1. **Concepts** with a diagram before any code.
2. **Mechanics**: what the protocol, runtime or database actually does.
3. **In code**: TypeScript (Node) and Python you can read and type yourself.
4. **Interview**: the questions you will be asked, with model answers and a rapid-fire list.
5. A three-question **check** before you mark the lesson done.

## The path

- **HTTP and API design**: the wire protocol, caching, REST design, authentication and authorisation.
- **The Node.js runtime and server architecture**: the event loop, workers, streams, layering, errors and configuration.
- **Data**: SQL, indexes and transactions, document modelling, caching.
- **Production**: queues and background jobs, testing, security, deployment and observability.

## How to study

- Build alongside: a small orders API with auth, pagination and a queue exercises every chapter. Pair it with the *Node backend* and *API design* topics in the daily plan.
- After each lesson, close the page and explain the main diagram aloud in two minutes.
- Answer the interview questions out loud before reading the model answers.

Your progress here is separate from the daily plan and never affects your streak.

courses.title: Computer Science Core
courses.blurb: The fundamentals every engineer is asked about: operating systems (processes, memory, concurrency), computer networks, database internals and transactions, and object-oriented design with SOLID and design patterns.
courses.audience: Anyone preparing for CS-fundamentals rounds, or filling gaps in their foundations
courses.intro:
## What this course is for

CS-fundamentals rounds are where candidates with the same projects separate: can you explain **what the machine, the network and the database are really doing** when your code runs? This course covers the four subjects interviewers return to again and again, taught for understanding rather than memorising definitions.

## The four parts

1. **Operating systems**: processes and threads, scheduling, virtual memory, synchronisation and deadlocks.
2. **Computer networks**: layers, IP, TCP in depth, DNS, TLS and the journey of a URL.
3. **Database internals**: storage engines, B-trees and LSM-trees, normalisation, transactions, isolation and recovery.
4. **Object-oriented design**: the four pillars, SOLID, and the design patterns that appear in real codebases and LLD interviews.

## How each lesson works

1. **Concept** in plain words, with a diagram or a worked example you can trace by hand.
2. **Mechanics**: what the kernel, protocol or engine actually does.
3. **Code** you can run: Python, Java, Go, C++ or JavaScript.
4. **Interview**: the questions you will be asked, with model answers and a rapid-fire list.
5. A three-question **check** before you mark the lesson done.

## How to study

- Take the subjects in any order, but lessons inside a subject build on each other.
- Always trace the worked examples by hand (address translation, round-robin scheduling, a deadlock cycle). Interviewers ask you to do exactly that.
- Pair each lesson with the matching topic in your daily plan (OS, networking, DBMS, OOP) so the daily quiz reinforces it.

Your progress here is separate from the daily plan and never affects your streak.

courses.title: JavaScript & TypeScript Deep Dive
courses.blurb: The language behind most of the web, understood properly: scope and closures, this and prototypes, coercion, the event loop and promises, async patterns, generators and modules, then the TypeScript type system from narrowing to generics.
courses.audience: Developers who use JavaScript daily and want to explain it, not just write it
courses.intro:
## What this course is for

JavaScript interviews are mostly **output-prediction and explain-why** questions: what does this print, why does `this` vanish, why does this promise log after that timeout? Candidates who learned the language through frameworks stumble because they have never built an accurate model of the engine. This course builds that model, then adds TypeScript on top.

## The three parts

1. **Language core**: execution contexts, scope, hoisting and closures; `this`, prototypes, classes and `new`; values, references, coercion and equality.
2. **Asynchronous JavaScript**: the event loop, microtasks and promises; async/await with cancellation, retries and concurrency limits; iterators, generators and modules.
3. **TypeScript**: structural typing, unions and narrowing, generics, utility, mapped and conditional types, and configuration for real projects.

## How each lesson works

1. **Concept** with small snippets you can paste into a console.
2. **Mechanics**: the rules the engine follows, stated precisely.
3. **Code**: realistic helpers (once, memoize, mapLimit, retry, typed emitter) you can reuse.
4. **Interview**: questions with model answers and a rapid-fire list.
5. A three-question **check** before you mark the lesson done.

## How to study

- Run every snippet and predict the output **before** you run it. Wrong predictions are where learning happens.
- Re-implement `bind`, `new`, `Promise.all`, `debounce` and `memoize` from memory; they are standard live-coding questions.
- Pair the lessons with the JavaScript and TypeScript topics in your daily plan and the JS challenges in the problem bank.

Your progress here is separate from the daily plan and never affects your streak.

courses.title: DevOps & Cloud
courses.blurb: Linux and Git fluency, Docker and Kubernetes from first principles, CI/CD pipelines and release strategies, infrastructure as code with Terraform, and the core AWS building blocks, IAM and cost control.
courses.audience: Developers who ship code and want to understand how it is built, deployed and run
courses.intro:
## What this course is for

Every engineer is expected to ship and operate what they build. DevOps interviews ask how you would **deploy, scale, secure and debug** a service, not for a list of tool names. This course teaches the mechanics under the tools so the answers stay valid when the tools change.

## The path

1. **Linux and Git**: the shell, permissions, processes and text tools; Git's object model, merge vs rebase, workflows and recovery.
2. **Containers and orchestration**: what a container really is, Docker images and production Dockerfiles, Kubernetes objects, probes, scaling and debugging.
3. **Delivery and cloud**: CI/CD pipelines, release strategies and supply-chain security; Terraform state, modules and safe changes; AWS compute, storage, networking, IAM and cost.

## How each lesson works

1. **Concept** with the problem the tool solves.
2. **Mechanics**: how it works underneath, with the commands and config you will actually write.
3. **Code**: Dockerfiles, YAML, HCL and shell you can copy and adapt.
4. **Interview**: questions with model answers, a debugging checklist and a rapid-fire list.
5. A three-question **check** before you mark the lesson done.

## How to study

- Do it, not just read it: install Docker, run a local Kubernetes cluster (kind or minikube), write a pipeline for a toy repo, and apply a small Terraform stack to a free-tier account.
- Break things on purpose (kill a pod, fill a disk, corrupt a rebase) and recover; that is what the interviews probe.
- Pair with the *Backend Engineering* course for deployment, observability and security from the application side.

Your progress here is separate from the daily plan and never affects your streak.

courses.title: Python Deep Dive
courses.blurb: Python beyond the syntax: names and mutability, the data model and dataclasses, iterators, generators and decorators, the GIL with threads, processes and asyncio, and profiling, testing and project tooling.
courses.audience: Developers who write Python and want to explain why it behaves the way it does
courses.intro:
## What this course is for

Python interviews and code reviews keep returning to a small set of questions: why did this default argument remember its last value, what does the GIL actually stop, when do I reach for asyncio, how do I make this faster? The answers all come from Python's **object model** and runtime. This course builds that model and then applies it.

## The two parts

1. **Python core**: names, objects and mutability, memory management; the data model (dunder methods, dataclasses, context managers, typing); iterators, generators, comprehensions and decorators.
2. **Python in practice**: concurrency with the GIL, threads, processes and asyncio; profiling and performance; testing with pytest; project tooling.

## How each lesson works

1. **Concept** with short snippets you can paste into a REPL.
2. **Mechanics**: what CPython actually does.
3. **Code**: realistic helpers (retry decorator, batching generator, timing context manager, async fan-out with limits).
4. **Interview**: questions with model answers and a rapid-fire list.
5. A three-question **check** before you mark the lesson done.

## How to study

- Predict the output of every snippet before running it.
- Re-write the examples from memory: a retry decorator, a context manager, a dataclass with a safe default, an asyncio fan-out with a semaphore.
- Pair the course with the Python solutions in the problem bank, and with the *Backend Engineering* course for production concerns.

Your progress here is separate from the daily plan and never affects your streak.
